paper_title: InterMimicGen: Scaling Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Self-Evolving Motion Imitation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Captured human-object interactions provide rich supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation, but they are sparse, heterogeneous, and not directly executable by robots. We introduce InterMimicGen, a self-evolving motion-imitation framework in which robot motion data and a tracking policy improve each other. First, we consolidate motion-captured human-object interaction datasets and retarget them into humanoid robot references while preserving whole-body coordination and dexterous hand-object relationships. This produces a large and diverse humanoid robot reference collection for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation. Second, we train a physics-based generalist tracker that executes these references in simulation on a humanoid with dexterous hands, covering a scale and diversity beyond prior humanoid tracking systems for loco-manipulation. Third, we close a data flywheel: each round makes small, task-preserving changes to where an interaction takes place and how the body performs it, fine-tunes the tracker on them, and keeps only the variants whose simulated execution completes the task, which seed the next round. With more iterations, these small edits compound into broader coverage around the sparse original demonstrations while preserving task semantics and motion quality. Experiments show contact-preserving retargeting across robot configurations, broad tracking with a single generalist policy, executable motions that keep growing over augmentation rounds, and transfer to real robots. InterMimicGen provides a unified path from heterogeneous human demonstrations to a continually expanding motion resource for humanoid robot learning.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The value of human demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation extends beyond reproducing the trajectories they record. Each demonstration captures one coordinated solution in high-dimensional 1 interaction space, but even large motion-capture corpus provides sparse samples of this space rather than dense coverage of their feasible variations. Covering these variations therefore requires either policy that can infer the physically feasible manifold from these sparse samples, or data-generation process that enriches the data with coordinated, physically valid variations. natural route is to train tracking policy by collecting more references, but any fixed set of references still leaves these variations uncovered. When we look back, generalist trackers already generalize well in locomotion (Luo et al., 2026), where motion close to demonstration usually remains feasible. Loco-manipulation is less forgiving. The robot must hold contact with an object while keeping its balance, so small change in posture or object placement can break grasp, push the hand into the object, or make the robot fall. As result, tracker that executes demonstration may still fail on the same task where the trajectory is shifted by only few centimeters (Sec. 4.4). Covering them therefore requires data that grows with the tracker rather than fixed collection. We build this as data flywheel, in which executable data and the tracker grow together. To instantiate this flywheel, we introduce InterMimicGen, self-evolving motion-imitation data engine that couples human-object interaction retargeting, large-scale motion imitation, and iterative data expansion. We first consolidate heterogeneous human-object motion-capture data (Figure 3) and retarget the interactions into humanoid robot references. Our retargeter keeps both long-horizon bodyobject relations and the finger contact that holds small objects: whole-body solver shapes the grasp to follow the objects geometry rather than captured finger poses alone, and fine-grained cleanup then refines the contact at the millimeter scale. The result is large and diverse robot reference collection for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation, as shown in Figure 1. Physics-based trackers then execute these references in simulation on humanoid robot with dexterous hands, and the same trackers later grow together with their reference data through iterative data expansion. The goal of this expansion is not to invent new tasks; each human interaction becomes seed for physically distinct realizations of the same semantic behavior, in the spirit of MimicGens demonstration-driven data expansion (Mandlekar et al., 2023). We vary object and body motion through small edits around previously validated interactions, such as placing box farther left or crouching more deeply. Each round fine-tunes the tracker on the current references and edited candidates, executes the candidates in simulation, and retains only rollouts that complete without failure. Drawing on InterMimics insight that policy can correct imperfect motion by learning from it (Xu et al., 2025d), imitation repairs errors introduced by the edits. The successful rollouts then seed the next round. This feedback is the defining step of InterMimicGen: corrected motions expand the reference set, and the expanded set enables the tracker to realize progressively larger variations. Our contributions are threefold. First, we consolidate heterogeneous human-object interaction (HOI) data and retarget them into, to our knowledge, the most diverse humanoid robot reference collection (see Sec. 4.1) for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation. Second, using these references, we train physics-based generalist tracker that realizes this repertoire on target embodiment at scale beyond prior humanoid tracking systems (Weng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026b) for loco-manipulation. Third, we introduce self-evolving augmentation-learning loop that expands this repertoire through coupled variations in object and whole-body motions, turning validated interactions into growing resource for subsequent learning of whole-body controllers.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Human-object interaction data. Human-object and human-scene capture datasets provide complementary interaction references across whole-body grasping, object tracking, bimanual manipulation, and scene-level coordination (Taheri et al., 2020; Bhatnagar et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024; Lv et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2023a; Zhao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023). These resources differ in object diversity, contact structure, and body and hand annotation, shaping the supervision available for imitation. Among them, InterAct (Xu et al., 2025c) consolidates heterogeneous interaction sources, while HiPHI (Ji et al., 2026) adds extensive body-object capture. We combine their motion into robot reference collection and expand physically executable coverage through retargeting and humanoid robot execution in simulation. Whole-body and dexterous motion retargeting. Motion retargeting adapts demonstrations across morphologies using learned mappings or optimization objectives built from skeleton structure, contact 2 cues, and geometric correspondences (Villegas et al., 2018; Aberman et al., 2020; Villegas et al., 2021; Reda et al., 2023; Araújo et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2026a). For interaction, the relationships between body, object, hand, and scene must survive the change in embodiment rather than only the joint trajectory (Kim et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2023b; Yang et al., 2026). Dexterous teleoperation and synthesis study high-quality hand or hand-arm transfer (Handa et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b), but whole-body interaction also requires those contacts to remain consistent with locomotion and balance. Our retargeter therefore separates the problem into coarse whole-body interaction solve and local dense contact refinement, so hand motion is improved without disturbing the body-object motion. Physics-based imitation and whole-body manipulation. Physics-based imitation began with example-guided control of individual skills (Peng et al., 2018) and later scaled to shared controllers over diverse motion libraries (Won et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2023). On physical humanoids, teleoperation and imitation enable whole-body control (He et al., 2024; Ze et al., 2025), while universal tracking policies and visuomotor extensions broaden the motion and sensing interfaces (Yin et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2025). Object-centric extensions couple body and object dynamics for grasping and dynamic skills (Wang et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Tessler et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025d; 2026a), and then move to real-world humanoid loco-manipulation (Weng et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025a; Dao et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Kalaria et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; He et al., 2026). Our work starts from reference tracking and extends it into self-evolving data engine, with real deployment. Demonstration augmentation and iterative generation. demonstration can be reused beyond its recorded trajectory (Mandlekar et al., 2023): collected segments preserve task intent, while execution under adapted conditions becomes valid training data. Later systems extend this execution-validated reuse to bimanual dexterity (Jiang et al., 2025), skill composition (Garrett et al., 2024), interventiondriven data collection (Hoque et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025), policy self-improvement (Bousmalis et al., 2024), and humanoid loco-manipulation (Lin et al., 2026). related line in character and humanoid control scales policies through generated experience or closed-loop motion generation (Xu et al., 2025a; Debbad et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026). Our setting differs in both domain and mechanism: we expand dexterous and agile humanoid loco-manipulation from motion-capture references, and we self-evolve through motion imitation itself instead of separate kinematic motion synthesizer, which is often brittle for object interaction.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: InterMimicGen turns captured human-object interactions into an expanding collection of robot references that physics-based tracker can execute (Figure 2). reference ξ stores the target robot motion, object motion, and contact intent of one clip. We first consolidate heterogeneous captures (Sec. 3.1) and retarget them to robot embodiments (Sec. 3.2). generalist tracker then realizes these references under robot dynamics (Sec. 3.3). Finally, self-evolving motion imitation edits how verified interactions are realized and keeps only the edits that the tracker executes in physics. Repeating this over rounds, with tracker that keeps learning from the new motions, lets the verified references and the tracker grow together (Sec. 3.4). 3.1 CONSOLIDATED INTERACTION REFERENCE COLLECTION Because our learning loop expands skills already represented in the source motions, the seed collection should cover interaction semantics as broadly as possible. We combine InterAct (Xu et al., 2025c) and the object-interaction portion of HiPHI (Ji et al., 2026) into shared collection. InterAct contributes diverse tasks and object categories by consolidating public motion-capture datasets (Taheri et al., 2020; Bhatnagar et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023a; Zhao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023), while HiPHI contributes longer synchronized human-object motions. Figure 3 summarizes this complementarity: the sources occupy different distributions of human motion, object geometry, and interaction space, and their union improves coverage on external motion probes. We convert both sources to common body-object-hand representation and treat absent hand annotations as unknown rather than as evidence of no contact, and later refine the hand with retargeting. 3 Figure 2: Top: Reference construction. Human-object motion capture is retargeted into whole-body dexterous references, which physics-based tracker imitates to produce seed rollouts. Bottom: Selfevolving motion imitation. Each round augments verified references into candidates, fine-tunes the tracker on them, executes the candidates in physics, and retains only successful rollouts as seeds for the next round; Bottom right: UMAP embeddings (Sec. E.1) of accepted augmentations expanding. We then keep only the interactions each target robot can physically support. Sequences that simulation cannot represent, such as bag hanging with an unmodeled strap, are removed, and platforms without dexterous hands exclude interactions whose success depends on articulated finger contact. The resulting references share one format for downstream training (Sec. A). 3.2 RETARGETING FOR DEXTEROUS WHOLE-BODY INTERACTION Retargeting must satisfy constraints at two scales. The whole body must preserve support and bodyobject geometry over long horizons, while the hand must resolve millimeter-scale contact around small object regions. Optimizing both with one objective tends to loosen contact or over-constrain the body. We therefore solve the whole body first, with finger-opposition term that shapes the grasp, and then remove local artifacts in cleanup that preserves contact (Algorithm 1). Interaction-preserving whole-body retargeting. The coarse stage transfers body-object relationships through an interaction mesh (Yang et al., 2026) that connects sparse body landmarks with sampled object geometry, so matching the mesh preserves spatial interaction structure rather than only joint poses. It solves for the floating base and articulated body under the target robots constraints, with sparse hand landmarks placing the wrists and palms. Because different motion clips might fail under different local constraints, we use several constrained solvers in turn and keep the first feasible solution. The solve keeps the source object trajectory fixed and includes the finger-opposition term below, so the hands close around the object while the body is solved. Finger opposition. Surface proximity alone can let several fingertips settle on the same side of an object, which does not hold it. We therefore add an opposition term to the whole-body solve. For fingertip , let nt,f be the normalized displacement from its selected object-surface point to the fingertip at time t, and let nt,thumb be the same direction for the thumb: Ecover(qt) = (cid:88) Fe gt,f (cid:2)n t,thumbnt,f + m(cid:3)2 +, [x]+ = max(x, 0), (1) where Fe contains the supported thumb-finger pairs, gt,f activates pair once the thumb and finger approach the object, and sets the opposition margin. The term penalizes pairs whose directions are not sufficiently opposed, so fingers are promoted to approach from the side opposite the thumb. Geometry cleanup with contact preservation. The whole-body solve can still leave small penetrations, jitter, and contact drift. We therefore refine the robot and object trajectories with two successive Adam passes (Kingma & Ba, 2015). The first reduces robot-object, floor, and hand self-collision while regularizing deviation from the coarse motion, foot support, joint limits, and temporal smoothness. The second smooths the repaired trajectory under collision constraints and preserves hand-object relationships during contact. Each pass is retained only if its output satisfies deviation and quality 4 checks relative to its input. Robots without articulated fingers omit finger-specific terms. Sec. gives the objectives, acceptance checks, and solver settings.

sections.content: The generalist tracker turns kinematic references into physically executable motions, and later serves as the validator of augmented references. We train single policy πθ with proximal policy optimization (Schulman et al., 2017) across parallel environments, sharing parameters across motions and objects. sections.content: A human capture shows what an interaction achieves but only one way of performing it. We therefore generate new ways of performing the same interaction. This follows the spirit of MimicGen (Mandlekar et al., 2023), which turns one demonstration into many training examples by replaying it under new conditions and keeping the successful replays, and here the replay is motion imitation by our tracker. Each variant is derived from verified parent reference ξ and must keep four properties of the parent, which form the invariant set I: the interaction type, the intended contacts, the object, and the task outcome. Variants thus add new motions around each capture without changing its meaning. What an edit changes. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate four questions. (i) Can one retargeter preserve both long-horizon body-object relations and fine finger contact, and does this yield cleaner references than prior retargeters (Sec. 4.2)? (ii) How broadly can trackers execute these references across objects and embodiments, and which interactions remain hard (Sec. 4.3)? (iii) Does growing the data together with the tracker expand what it can execute beyond the original references, and does this growth come from learning rather than from filtering more rollouts (Sec. 4.4)? (iv) Do the resulting motions carry over from simulation to different real humanoid robots (Sec. 4.5)? 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Data and embodiments. We consolidate InterAct (Xu et al., 2025c) and HiPHI (Ji et al., 2026) into collection of 16,059 motions, 140.68 reference hours, and 157 object entries  (Table 4)  , which covers wide range of everyday interactions (Figure 3). We retarget it to six robot configurations: G1 (Unitree Robotics, b) with non-dexterous, Inspire (Inspire Robots), or Dex3 (Unitree Robotics, a) hands, Booster T1 and K1 (Booster Robotics, b;a), and Dexmate Vega (Dexmate). Sec. A.1 details which experiments run on each embodiment. Metrics. Each experiment uses its own group of metrics, and Sec. defines each of them once. Retargeted references are scored on plausibility and fidelity to the human motion: hand-contact preservation, in-hand slip, penetration, foot sliding, MPJPE, and joint acceleration. Tracking is scored by the success rate, the fraction of clips executed to the end without fall or large body, object, or interaction error, and by body and object errors on successful clips. For the augmentation loop, we report the growth of the verified reference set, the success of the tracker before and after self-evolution on the generated and original references, and the quality of their executions. Baselines. For dexterous retargeting, we compare with Weave (Cao et al., 2026b), whose released retargeted references use the same embodiment with InterMimicGen. For retargeting without dexterous hands, we compare with OmniRetarget (Yang et al., 2026), UMR (Cao et al., 2026a), and ULTRA (He et al., 2026) on G1. For tracking, no publicly available tracker is trained on an interaction collection of comparable scale, so we compare our generalist with per-object specialists, each trained only on the references of one object, which serve as practical upper bound. We ask three questions: are the augmented references of good quality, does each round expand their range, and does training on them improve the tracker? We replay every accepted reference and every original reference with the tracker before and after self-evolution, counting reference as executed when at least one of three rollouts reaches its end (success columns of Table 3). The original tracker fails on more than third of the accepted references even though it is trained with large-scale data, whereas the evolved tracker executes nearly all of them, and both execute every original reference. Self-evolution therefore extends what the tracker can execute without losing what it could already do. 4.5 CROSS-EMBODIMENT EXECUTION AND REAL-WORLD TRANSFER To verify that the trajectories produced by InterMimicGen work beyond simulation, we execute them on real robots. Each embodiment uses the parts of the framework it supports (Sec. A.1), and each platform runs its own low-level controller, trained by us or publicly available (Sec. G). These controllers are blind to the object and track only the robot motion, yet our trajectories execute well on every platform, suggesting that they are physically consistent enough to transfer without object feedback. sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: InterMimicGen treats humanoid tracker as both consumer and producer of interaction data. consolidated human-object motion collection supplies diverse task semantics, hand-aware retargeting transfers them to six robot configurations, and physics-based tracking grounds them in executable motion. The evolving loop then turns validated variations into new references. Every round enlarges the archive, and the fine-tuned tracker learns interactions beyond the base trackers reach while keeping its seed skills. Learning is what keeps the loop going, since frozen tracker stops accepting new variations after the first round. 9 Acknowledgments. We thank Ziyin Wang for helping with the on-site deployment.

We set λI = 10, uniform over the mesh vertices. Etemporal penalizes the squared change of each coordinate of qt from the previous frames solution, with weight 2 for the floating base, legs, and waist and 1 for the arm and finger joints. Eposture penalizes the waist yaw and roll angles with weight 0.2 each. Sparse hand landmarks place the wrist and palm, and the opposition term Ecover of Eq. 1 shapes the fingers, with weight λC = 3 and margin = 1. Because the cosine between two directions is at least 1, this margin keeps the term active for every active pair, so the term pulls each pair toward full opposition. When opposition is active. The switch gt,f turns the opposition term on only when grasp is forming. It activates when the thumb and at least one other finger are within 10 cm of the object, holds for 15 frames, and resets only after the fingers move more than 15 cm away. Contact labels in the reference can also trigger it. Solvers. Different clips fail under different local constraints and solvers, so we solve the same interaction-mesh objective with several constrained solvers, tried in turn: MOSEK, Clarabel, ECOS, CVXOPT, OSQP, and SCS, plus box-bound variants of Clarabel, OSQP, and SCS that replace the local Euclidean step bound with componentwise bounds. The coarse stage is solved frame by frame, warm-started from the previous frame. The first solution that passes the feasibility checks initializes the cleanup stage. Surface correspondences. The opposition term needs an object-surface point for every active fingertip. For fingertip landmark pt,f and selected object-surface point st,f on the objects collision geometry, we define vt,f = pt,f st,f and the direction nt,f = vt,f /vt,f of Eq. 1. The term depends on the robot configuration through the wrist and hand forward kinematics and is purely geometric: it compares the thumb direction with each active opposing fingertip direction, which pushes the fingers to contact the object from complementary sides. Both passes are strongly regularized toward their input. Table 6 lists the default weights. Penetration repair runs 300 Adam and 60 projection steps. It penalizes robot-object penetration with 2 mm clearance margin, robot-floor and object-floor penetration, and hand self-collision beyond the overlap already present in its input, while fidelity and smoothness terms keep the edit small and free of new roughness. Collision-aware smoothing then runs 400 Adam and 60 projection steps. It penalizes acceleration and jerk of the body, hands, root, object, and body landmarks, keeps the collision penalties so that smoothing cannot reintroduce penetration, and weakens data fidelity to 0.02 at frames with sudden hand jumps so that these jumps can be smoothed away. How contact is preserved. Two terms protect contact. In both passes, contact-keeping term penalizes robot points that were near contact in the input and move more than 2 cm away from the object. Smoothing also keeps the hand-base pose fixed relative to the object at frames in contact, detected as an object distance below 1.5 cm, with relative-pose scale of 2 cm. These terms preserve and stabilize existing contact but do not attract fingertips to new surface points. Grasp shape comes from the opposition term of the whole-body solve. Acceptance checks. Each pass accepts candidate only after the complete trajectory passes its check against that passs input: the repair check compares with the whole-body solution, and the smoothing check compares with the repaired trajectory  (Table 7)  . The checks bound how far the root, joints, object, and body may move, how much penetration may grow, and how many contact frames must survive, which applies when the input has at least five. Repair must also improve penetration: if the inputs maximum penetration exceeds 3 mm, the output must reach at most 3 mm or cut that maximum by at least 25%. Smoothing must not worsen the aggregate jerk score. Jerk limits allow each metric to grow by the listed factor plus small fixed margin. Both checks reject nonfinite results, quaternion-norm errors of at least 106, new joint-limit violations, and objects that sink more than 5 mm below their starting height or the floor. Retargeting to wheeled robots. For wheeled embodiments such as the Dexmate Vega, we keep the interaction-mesh objective and adapt the configuration space and landmark correspondences. The planar base translation and yaw are optimized jointly with the upper body, while the chassis height stays at its nominal value and the base roll and pitch are fixed at zero. Human leg and foot landmarks are removed from the interaction mesh and the foot-contact constraints are disabled, so the base, torso, and arms together preserve the demonstrated manipulation without passing changes in human pelvis height to the chassis. The three torso joints are constrained only through the mapped shoulder, elbow, 17 wrist, and hand landmarks rather than by matching human spine angles. Temporal regularization and bounds on frame-to-frame changes of the upper-body joints and the planar base limit abrupt motion, and the wheel joints stay fixed during this kinematic stage. We discuss how the trajectories can be used by the real controller in Sec. G.

sections.title: E EVALUATION METRICS
sections.content: This section defines each metric of Sec. 4.1 once, grouped in the order of the experiments: data coverage (Figure 3), retargeted references (Sec. 4.2), tracking (Sec. 4.3), and the augmentation loop (Sec. 4.4). All compared methods share the same features, thresholds, and frame rates. E.1 DATA COVERAGE The panels of Figure 2 and Figure 3 are computed from the following features. Human motion. Each sequence is described by 21 non-finger joint positions relative to the pelvis, normalized by skeletal height, plus root displacement, height, and heading. Each channel is resampled to 128 frames and truncated to its first 16 DCT coefficients (1,088 dimensions), and PCA-64 then UMAP-2 gives one point per sequence (16,059). The feature uses no object information. 21 Object geometry. Each mesh is sampled with 10,000 surface points, centered, scaled to the unit sphere, and oriented by its first source pose, then embedded with frozen OpenShape PointBERT encoder; embeddings are averaged over four yaw rotations. PCA and UMAP give one point per distinct geometry (155). Unit-sphere scaling removes physical size. Human-object interaction. The feature concatenates the object position relative to the pelvis, the wrist positions and surface distances relative to the object, the wrist separation, and the object height, translation, and rotation, encoded with the same DCT scheme. Each block is normalized separately before PCA-64 and UMAP-2. External coverage. Probes from GRAIL, MOVIN, and ELMO are matched to the source library in 73-dimensional body-motion space: PCA-64 of the pelvis-relative joint DCT features plus nine per-limb repetition descriptors. probe is covered when its nearest source sequence lies within the 75th percentile of the source leave-one-out nearest-neighbor distance, and coverage averages the three probe sets equally. We compare the full InterAct, HiPHI, and their union without subsampling. Scaling. Coverage is computed on nested random subsets of the union and averaged over 20 orderings; shading marks the 5th95th percentiles. E.2 RETARGETED REFERENCES These metrics score kinematic references in Table 1 and Table 10. Each method is evaluated on its own robot model at 30 fps, on the source clips shared by the compared methods, against the human reference scaled by the subjects body scale. Contact preservation. During human-labeled hand contact, hand preserves contact when the minimum distance between its wrist, palm, and finger meshes and the object mesh is at most 2 cm, with interpenetration counted as zero. The per-frame variant requires all contacting hands to be preserved; the per-hand variant counts each handframe separately. In-hand slip. Mean speed of eleven hand keypoints in the object frame over consecutive contact frames. Penetration. frame penetrates when any robot collision geometry is deeper than 1 cm inside the object (a shared 20-part convex decomposition). We report their mean maximum depth. Ground penetration (Gnd.) is the fraction of frames in which any robot collision geometry is more than 1 cm below the floor. Sliding-frame speed is the mean robot toe speed over sliding frames. Fidelity. HARDWARE AND REAL-WORLD DEPLOYMENT Deployment for Unitree G1. Experiments are performed on Unitree G1 humanoid with 29 DOFs (six per leg, three at the waist, and seven per arm), running robot firmware version 1.5.4. The policy is executed on laptop with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 Laptop GPU and communicates over Ethernet through Unitrees SDK. We use SONIC (Luo et al., 2026) as the low-level whole-body controller: it takes the reference motion at 50 Hz, which is tracked by the onboard joint-level PD controllers at 500 Hz, using SONICs default per-joint PD gains. On top of these, stiffness and damping scales of 1.5 are applied to the two ankle pitch motors; constant 1 degree pitch offset is further added to the measured pelvis IMU orientation to account for the calibration bias of the robots own IMU. Deployment for Unitree G1 with Inspire dexterous hands. For tasks that require dexterous manipulation, we equip Unitree G1 with two Inspire RH56DFTP dexterous hands, each with six actuated DOFs, plus six mimic joints. The humanoid body is controlled by SONIC as described above, while the hands directly replay the finger trajectory of the rollout motion. For the synchronization, the body deployment publishes its current playback frame, and separate process sends the hand pose for that frame to the robot at about 12 Hz. Notably, we initiate the thumb motion first, followed by the motion of the other four fingers. Deployment for Booster K1. Experiments are performed on Booster K1 humanoid with 22 DOFs (six per leg, four per arm, and two at the head). For policy training, we build on Booster Train (https://github.com/BoosterRobotics/booster_train), extending it with object-interaction tracking and targeted domain randomization. We use an asymmetric actor-critic formulation, with privileged object and contact information provided only to the critic during training. Robot and object dynamics are randomized, including ground friction, object mass, center of mass, object placement, actuator properties, and external perturbations, while preserving close tracking of the reference body and object motion. For real-world execution, policies are deployed using Booster Deploy (https://github.com/BoosterRobotics/booster_deploy). Deployment for Dexmate Vega. Experiments are performed on Dexmate Vega-1 Pro, bimanual mobile manipulator with 23 DOFs (three at the torso, seven per arm, three at the head, and three DOFs at the omnidirectional wheeled base). Since the wheeled base is stable and agile, no whole-body controller from RL is needed. Retargeted upper-body joint trajectories are sent directly to the onboard joint controllers through Dexmates dexcontrol SDK (v0.5.0). Notably, due to the torso joint speed limit, all trajectories are uniformly time-scaled by 0.3 speed during deployment. Base motion is converted to wheel commands by solving the chassis inverse kinematics using trajectory optimization, formulated in CasADi (Andersson et al., 2019) and solved with IPOPT (Wächter & Biegler, 2006). The solver penalizes position, yaw, terminal-pose tracking errors, and regularizes body acceleration, steering rate and acceleration, and wheel acceleration. All commands are streamed at 100 Hz.

sections.title: H LIMITATIONS
sections.content: The loop varies how an interaction is realized, so it densifies coverage around each demonstration without creating new task semantics. Iterative selection may also favor easier objects or compound reference errors.
